title: Strong Foundations, Strong Futures: Leadership Driving Education Reform Across Africa
author: Nomawethu Matshingana
excerpt: The education sector in South Africa and across the continent continues to experience important leadership-driven developments focused on strengthening systems, improving outcomes, and preparing institutions for future challenges.
body: The education sector in South Africa and across the continent continues to experience important leadership-driven developments focused on strengthening systems, improving outcomes, and preparing institutions for future challenges.

The Department of Basic Education (DBE), in partnership with Canva and other private sector partners, is preparing to host the 12th National Education Excellence Awards (NEEAs) on 24 July in Sandton. Under the theme "Strong Foundations, Strong Futures," the awards will recognise outstanding district leadership, operational excellence, and high-performing public schools across all quintiles from the 2025 National Senior Certificate (NSC) cycle. The event will bring together key education leaders, including Minister Siviwe Gwarube, Deputy Minister Dr Reginah Mhaule, and Director-General Mathanzima Mweli, to celebrate achievements within the public education system.

In higher education, Universities South Africa (USAf) and the Department of Higher Education and Training (DHET) have shared key outcomes from the 2026 Entrepreneurial Executive Leadership Workshop. The discussions highlighted a growing shift among South Africa's 26 public universities towards embedding entrepreneurial thinking, innovation, and commercialisation into academic programmes. Rather than relying only on policy frameworks, university leaders are focusing on creating practical pathways that enable students and researchers to transform intellectual property and innovative ideas into market-ready solutions through stronger partnerships with industry.

Across Africa and globally, there is increasing recognition that effective school leadership is a specialised professional discipline and a vital driver of education transformation. The African Centre for School Leadership (ACSL) recently presented evidence at UNESCO IIEP's Strategic Debate, reinforcing the need to develop dedicated leadership pathways for school leaders beyond traditional teaching roles. This aligns with commitments by African education ministers to strengthen leadership development as a foundation for improving education systems. At UNESCO's global education discussions in Paris, President Cyril Ramaphosa also called for greater investment in foundational education and institutional capacity to ensure sustainable progress for future generations.

title: Higher Education Governance, Education Reform & Foundational Learning
author: Nomawethu Matshingana
excerpt: South Africa's education sector continues to navigate significant leadership, governance and policy developments as government, universities and education stakeholders work to strengthen institutions, improve accountability and enhance learning outcomes across the system.
body: South Africa's education sector continues to navigate significant leadership, governance and policy developments as government, universities and education stakeholders work to strengthen institutions, improve accountability and enhance learning outcomes across the system.

In higher education, governance and student funding remain under the spotlight. Parliament has criticised Student Representative Councils (SRCs) from institutions including Wits, UCT, UJ and Stellenbosch after they jointly opposed the National Student Financial Aid Scheme (NSFAS) accommodation cap of R52,000. Tebogo Letsie, Chairperson of Parliament's Portfolio Committee on Higher Education and Training, urged student leaders to prioritise demanding greater transparency from universities regarding accommodation pricing rather than defending rising costs. Meanwhile, Higher Education Minister Buti Manamela has appointed an independent assessor at the University of Venda following ongoing governance disputes, leadership instability and the precautionary suspension of senior university executives. The intervention is expected to provide recommendations aimed at restoring effective governance and institutional stability.

The basic education sector is simultaneously facing pressing workforce and policy challenges. Newly released parliamentary data by Basic Education Minister Siviwe Gwarube indicates that nearly half of South Africa's state-employed educators are aged 50 years or older, raising concerns about a looming teacher replacement crisis. With provinces such as the Western Cape and Northern Cape continuing to experience high vacancy rates, government is under increasing pressure to strengthen teacher recruitment, retention and development strategies. The Department of Basic Education has also issued Circular S7 of 2026, reaffirming every learner's constitutional right to education regardless of nationality while warning communities and external groups against unauthorised inspections and vigilantism at public schools. In addition, amendments to the South African Schools Act are being developed to formally regulate online schools and modernise the country's home education framework, with draft regulations expected to be released for public comment.

Alongside these reforms, government is accelerating efforts to improve foundational learning outcomes. Following the national launch of the Literacy Promotion Toolkit earlier this month, provincial education departments and district leadership teams have begun implementing training to institutionalise structured reading practices across primary schools. At the same time, the Department of Basic Education is expanding literacy and numeracy training to 10,000 Foundation Phase educators while reducing administrative burdens on teachers, enabling them to dedicate more time to classroom instruction and improving learner achievement.

title: Education Reform, Skills Development & Global Learning
author: Nomawethu Matshingana
excerpt: South Africa's education landscape continues to evolve through a series of leadership-driven reforms aimed at improving quality, strengthening governance and preparing learners for the demands of a rapidly changing world.
body: South Africa's education landscape continues to evolve through a series of leadership-driven reforms aimed at improving quality, strengthening governance and preparing learners for the demands of a rapidly changing world. From new approaches to measuring school performance to expanded skills development and growing international collaboration, education leaders are placing greater emphasis on long-term system improvement.

The Department of Basic Education is introducing a more comprehensive approach to evaluating provincial matric performance through a new "Quality Basket" model. Rather than focusing only on overall pass rates, the framework will assess provinces using a broader set of indicators, including bachelor pass rates, learner retention, and participation and achievement in gateway subjects such as Mathematics, Physical Sciences and Accounting. The shift reflects a growing emphasis on measuring the overall quality and sustainability of education outcomes rather than examination results alone.

At the same time, the department continues to expand access to Early Childhood Development (ECD), with registered programmes now serving more than 1.2 million children nationwide. Alongside this expansion, government is rolling out new national screen-time guidelines for children between the ages of two and six, while strengthening nutrition initiatives aimed at reducing childhood stunting and improving school readiness. To support provinces facing financial and operational challenges, specialised technical advisory teams have also been deployed to assist with budget planning, school resourcing and financial management.

Leadership within the post-school education and training sector is also gaining momentum. The Energy and Water Sector Education and Training Authority (EWSETA) has appointed Kedibone Moroane-Nkhobo as its new Chief Executive Officer, with a strong focus on expanding technical skills development, increasing artisan training and strengthening partnerships with industry to support South Africa's water and clean energy sectors. Meanwhile, the Department of Higher Education and Training has reiterated the need to accelerate artisan development after new figures showed that South Africa currently produces approximately 19,500 qualified artisans each year—well below the National Development Plan's target of 30,000 annually by 2030. Business and industry leaders continue to advocate for stronger apprenticeship programmes and expanded workplace learning opportunities to address the country's critical skills shortage.

Globally, education systems are placing greater emphasis on digital transformation and foundational learning. Following international leadership meetings in Paris, UNESCO, UNICEF and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) announced the expansion of the Gateways Initiative, which seeks to establish open-access digital learning platforms that promote equitable access to quality education while ensuring artificial intelligence supports critical thinking rather than widening the digital divide. South Africa also celebrated an international achievement in foundational literacy, with Team South Africa securing fourth place overall at the World Spelling Bee Championship in Shanghai, reflecting the country's growing competitiveness in global academic competitions.

title: Governance, Higher Education Support & Learner Excellence
author: Nomawethu Matshingana
excerpt: Leadership across South Africa's education sector continues to focus on strengthening governance, improving access to education and celebrating learner achievement, with new developments spanning civic engagement, higher education funding and investment in modern learning environments.
body: Leadership across South Africa's education sector continues to focus on strengthening governance, improving access to education and celebrating learner achievement, with new developments spanning civic engagement, higher education funding and investment in modern learning environments.

In a move to strengthen democratic participation ahead of the 2026 Local Government Elections, the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC), led by Chairperson Mosotho Moepya, met with the Royal Leaders of South Africa (ROLESA) at OR Tambo International Airport. The engagement centred on enhancing voter education, improving electoral readiness and working closely with traditional leaders to encourage greater participation in rural communities ahead of the 4 November elections. Meanwhile, in the Eastern Cape, Premier Oscar Mabuyane and Education MEC Fundile Gade officially handed over the newly built David Livingstone High School in Gqeberha. The state-of-the-art facility features modern science laboratories, digital media classrooms and upgraded sports facilities, reflecting the province's continued investment in improving education infrastructure and expanding learning opportunities for learners.

Within the higher education sector, government leadership continues to prioritise student access and financial support. Following interventions by Deputy Minister Yusuf Cassim and NSFAS Administrator Professor Hlengani Mathebula, specialised processing teams have been deployed to resolve more than 10,000 outstanding NSFAS appeal cases, helping thousands of university and TVET college students secure funding for second-semester registration. At the same time, the Department of Higher Education and Training has urged NSFAS to finalise funding allocations for mid-year admissions and improve the efficiency of monthly allowance payments to minimise disruptions to students and institutions.

South Africa also continues to celebrate excellence on the global stage. The North West Department of Education recently honoured 13-year-old Mbulelo Tolom of Klerksdorp Primary School after his outstanding performance at the World Spelling Bee Championship in Shanghai, China. As the youngest competitor in the tournament, Mbulelo achieved an impressive sixth-place individual finish, contributing to Team South Africa's fourth-place overall ranking and highlighting the country's growing strength in foundational literacy and international academic competition.

title: Research Excellence, Skills Development & Learner Well-being
author: Nomawethu Matshingana
excerpt: South Africa's education sector continues to advance through strategic leadership appointments, expanded skills development initiatives and programmes that promote learner well-being.
body: South Africa's education sector continues to advance through strategic leadership appointments, expanded skills development initiatives and programmes that promote learner well-being. These developments reflect a growing commitment to strengthening research, preparing young people for the future workforce and creating healthier learning environments.

In the higher education and research sector, the Academy of Science of South Africa (ASSAf) has announced new leadership appointments following nominations endorsed by the Minister of Science, Technology and Innovation, Professor Blade Nzimande. Professor Shireen Motala, the South African Research Chair in Teaching and Learning at the University of Johannesburg (UJ), has been appointed Vice-President of ASSAf, while UJ Vice-Chancellor and Principal, Professor Letlhokwa Mpedi, joins the ASSAf Council as a full member for the remainder of the 2024–2028 term. The appointments recognise the important role of academic leadership in advancing research, innovation and evidence-based policy across South Africa.

Efforts to strengthen the country's technical and digital skills pipeline are also gaining momentum. Ericsson South Africa has launched the first cohort of a five-year field operations learnership programme in KuGompo, East London, aimed at equipping young people with the practical skills needed to support the country's expanding digital infrastructure. Accredited by MICT SETA and the Quality Council for Trades and Occupations (QCTO), the 12-month programme combines classroom learning with workplace experience to qualify technicians and riggers at NQF Level 4. At the same time, government leaders, including Minister Mondli Gungubele, have renewed calls for technology companies and state-owned entities to expand structured workplace learning opportunities, apprenticeships and internships to help address South Africa's growing digital skills gap.

Supporting learner health remains an important priority across the basic education sector. Provincial education departments are introducing specialised training programmes that equip Foundation Phase educators to identify early signs of vision impairment, allowing learners to receive support before visual challenges affect their academic development. Meanwhile, integrated school health services continue to expand through ongoing HPV vaccination campaigns in Gauteng, where health and education officials are working together to improve preventative healthcare for learners and promote healthier school communities.

title: Education Excellence, Digital Transformation & Institutional Leadership
author: Nomawethu Matshingana
excerpt: Leadership across the education sector continues to shape the future of learning through excellence, innovation and strategic institutional development.
body: Leadership across the education sector continues to shape the future of learning through excellence, innovation and strategic institutional development. From recognising outstanding schools and educators to advancing digital transformation and strengthening university leadership, today's developments highlight a shared commitment to building more resilient and future-ready education systems.

In South Africa, the Department of Basic Education (DBE), in partnership with Canva, hosted the 12th Annual National Education Excellence Awards (NEEAs) in Sandton under the theme "Strong Foundations, Strong Futures." The awards celebrated outstanding school districts, education leaders and teaching innovations, while recognising excellence in Mathematics, Science, Accounting and school facility maintenance.

The University of Pretoria's E-Education Unit also received international recognition after winning the 2026 Blackboard Catalyst Award for Leading Change. The award acknowledges the University's leadership in successfully transitioning to digitally enabled teaching through its clickUP Ultra platform, setting a benchmark for higher education across Africa.

Meanwhile, the University of Venda (UNIVEN) honoured outgoing Registrar Dr Joel Baloyi for his dedicated service and leadership. His contributions to institutional governance, student affairs and transparency were recognised as an example of service-driven leadership in higher education.

Globally, the 8th World Congress of Education, held in Helsinki, Finland, brought together education leaders and researchers to explore the future of learning. Discussions focused on demographic trends, innovative teaching approaches, sustainable human capital development and new frameworks for measuring skills, supported by the Yidan Prize Foundation.

In Bengaluru, India, more than 100 education leaders gathered at the EduVision 2026 conclave, where they adopted a 10-point action agenda to accelerate the integration of artificial intelligence into K-12 education. The initiative promotes personalised digital learning, stronger school management practices and the responsible use of AI in classrooms.

Leadership transitions also featured prominently, with ESCP Business School appointing Professor Thomas Jeanjean as Executive President and Dean, while the Great Lakes Institute of Management appointed Raj Krishnan Shankar as its new Director.

title: Education Policy, Digital Transformation & Social Empowerment
author: Nomawethu Matshingana
excerpt: Leadership across South Africa's education and public institutions continues to evolve as leaders respond to the demands of digital transformation, inclusive education, youth development and stronger governance.
body: Leadership across South Africa's education and public institutions continues to evolve as leaders respond to the demands of digital transformation, inclusive education, youth development and stronger governance. Today's developments reflect a growing recognition that meaningful educational progress requires not only policy reform and institutional leadership, but also mentorship, innovation and opportunities for young people to participate in shaping the future.

The Association for Distance Education Providers and Online Schools (ADEPOS) is hosting its inaugural National Virtual Conference under the theme, "Seizing Opportunities, Addressing Urgency: Online Education in South Africa – Driving Policy Change for a Digital Future." The conference brings important attention to the rapid growth of online and distance education and the need for policies that keep pace with technological change. Discussions are focusing on legal and policy gaps, quality assurance frameworks involving Umalusi and SACAI, the digital divide, as well as the responsible integration of artificial intelligence and adaptive learning into mainstream schooling.

In the higher education and skills development space, Deputy Minister of Higher Education and Training, Dr Nomusa Dube-Ncube, is delivering the keynote address at the inaugural Post-School Education and Training (PSET) Research Conference in Umhlanga, KwaZulu-Natal. The conference highlights the importance of research and evidence in ensuring that South Africa's skills development priorities remain aligned with economic growth, employment opportunities and the changing needs of the country.

Student funding is also receiving high-level attention, with higher education leadership undertaking oversight visits to National Student Financial Aid Scheme (NSFAS) offices to address processing delays affecting the Funza Lushaka Bursary Programme for teacher education. Strengthening the administration of student funding remains essential, particularly for aspiring teachers whose studies contribute directly to the future of South Africa's education system.

Youth empowerment remains another important dimension of leadership development. The 25th "Empowering the Boychild" workshop at MC Weiler Primary School in Alexandra brought together more than 50 learners, business executives, academic leaders from the University of Johannesburg and the University of Pretoria, as well as representatives from the Gauteng Department of Basic Education. The initiative continues to create meaningful spaces for young men to develop emotional intelligence, confidence, personal responsibility and career awareness through mentorship and exposure to positive role models.

In Gqeberha, the Department of Correctional Services is concluding its two-day Women in Sport Empowerment Seminar, which places female leadership, personal development and social transformation at the centre of discussions. The initiative demonstrates how sport can become a powerful vehicle for building confidence, developing leadership capacity and supporting broader institutional reform.

The conversation around ethical leadership is also gaining momentum as media accreditation closes for the inaugural Nokuthula Simelane Memorial Lecture, hosted by the Nokuthula Simelane Foundation. The lecture is intended to create a national platform for emerging leaders to engage with questions of ethical governance, human rights and social justice — issues that remain fundamental to building accountable and compassionate institutions.

Taken together, these developments point to a South African education and leadership landscape that is increasingly focused on preparing people not simply to adapt to change, but to lead it. Whether through digital education, evidence-based policy, student support, youth mentorship, women's empowerment or ethical governance, today's initiatives reinforce the importance of leadership that is responsive, inclusive and grounded in service to society.

title: Education Excellence, Digital Transformation & Institutional Development
author: Nomawethu Matshingana
excerpt: Leadership and education remain deeply connected to the future of South Africa. Across schools, universities and education institutions, effective leadership is increasingly about more than administration.
body: Leadership and education remain deeply connected to the future of South Africa. Across schools, universities and education institutions, effective leadership is increasingly about more than administration. It is about improving teaching and learning, strengthening institutions, embracing technology and ensuring that every learner has a meaningful opportunity to succeed.

At school level, School Governing Bodies (SGBs) and School Management Teams (SMTs) continue to play an important role in strengthening institutional leadership. In many under-resourced public schools, effective governance and committed school leadership can make a significant difference in learner outcomes. The focus is gradually shifting from managing day-to-day operations to providing stronger instructional leadership — supporting teachers, improving curriculum delivery and using learning outcomes to guide decision-making.

Foundational literacy and numeracy remain among the most important priorities for educational leaders in South Africa. Early-grade reading comprehension and basic mathematical skills provide the foundation for future learning. Strong leadership at school and district level is therefore essential in ensuring that teachers receive the support, resources and professional development needed to address learning gaps.

Digital transformation is also changing the responsibilities of educational leaders. Initiatives such as the AFRETEC Teaching and Learning Framework, developed through partnerships among African universities including the University of the Witwatersrand, are placing greater emphasis on digital capacity, curriculum transformation, artificial intelligence and responsible technology governance.

However, digital transformation cannot be separated from the question of equity. South Africa continues to experience a significant digital divide between well-resourced urban and private schools and many rural and township institutions. Educational leaders therefore face the dual responsibility of embracing innovation while ensuring that technology does not deepen existing inequalities.

Higher education is experiencing a similar transformation. Universities are under increasing pressure to modernise their curricula and prepare students for a rapidly changing world of work. Leadership in this environment requires institutions to respond to emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, data, digital technologies and entrepreneurship, while remaining responsive to local communities and South Africa's broader economic needs.

Leadership development is also receiving increased attention through academic conferences, education summits and professional gatherings taking place across South Africa and internationally. These platforms provide opportunities for educators, researchers, policymakers and institutional leaders to exchange ideas on educational innovation, governance, social development and the future of learning.

Values-based leadership remains particularly important. Effective educational leadership is ultimately not only about performance indicators and institutional targets; it is also about integrity, accountability, inclusion and service. Leaders who understand the communities they serve are better positioned to create institutions where educators feel supported and learners are given the opportunity to thrive.

As South Africa continues to navigate curriculum reform, digital transformation and persistent inequalities, the role of educational leadership will become even more significant. The future of education will depend not only on new policies and technologies, but on leaders who can translate those changes into meaningful improvements in classrooms, institutions and communities.

The intersection of leadership and education is therefore not simply about managing change. It is about providing a clear vision for the future, empowering people and building an education system that is more equitable, innovative, resilient and prepared for the generations to come.
